Every session rates the same human answers, so S1 to S3 also share that arm. sample_overlap should name Charness and Grieco (2019).

corrections.source_says: The paper names the creativity score as its main outcome variable, so the six creativity outcomes (S1-O1, S1-O2, S2-O1, S2-O2, S3-O1, S3-O2) are at least paper_primary. The public AsPredicted entries cited on p. 1 support preregistered_primary: #136955 gives 'Creativity levels (score in the range 1-10)' as the key dependent variable, and #194851 and #225528 give 'Creativity levels, plus 1 (originality), 2 (elaboration), 3 (nonsense)'. The four originality outcomes are secondary in the paper's framing, although the follow-up preregistrations list originality among the key variables.
corrections.quote: use creativity scores assigned by external judges as the main outcome variable

The gap (0.339) is less than twice either printed standard error, so the source does not show a clear AI advantage in closed-task originality in Session II. no_clear_difference fits better, or the record should say the direction rests on point estimates alone. S3-O3 (6.600 vs 5.839) also has no test, but its gap is large next to the standard errors.

confirmed: Version: the PDF on file is the 19-page manuscript dated January 21, 2026 (p. 1), with main text and references only (references pp. 17-19) and no appendices. Crossref confirms doi 10.1093/ej/ueag015 as 'Creativity and AI' by Charness and Grieco, The Economic Journal, journal-article, online 2026-01-28. The DOI is not printed in the PDF; it comes from the search record and Crossref.
Title 'CREATIVITY AND AI' and authors Gary Charness and Daniela Grieco match p. 1.

Design and context class ai_vs_human for S1 to S3: a 2x2 design of task openness by producer (humans vs. GPT), with 738 Prolific subjects rating answers without being told that AI could have produced them (p. 4, Section 2.1; p. 5, fn. 4). The human answers come from a 2019 laboratory experiment, and no person used AI.

No randomized people study: the only randomization is the random draw of six answers (three human, three AI) for each rater from the 80 in a sub-session (p. 4). The text does not say how raters were split between the Closed and Open sub-sessions, as the notes say. Section 4 has GPT rate the answers, with no people using AI (p. 15).
No diversity outcome: the paper computes no similarity or diversity measure across outputs. 'Diversity' appears only in interpretation (p. 12) and in a citation of Girotra et al. (p. 9).

Counts: 738 recruited instead of 720 planned (p. 4; p. 5, fn. 5); 4428 evaluations, 1506 + 1482 + 1440, with the third labelled 'in the second' (p. 5); Table 1 Subj. 128/123, 119/119, 122/119, summing to 251, 238, 241 and 730 (p. 7); 40 human and 40 GPT answers per task in each session (pp. 5-6). Six evaluations per rater fit Session I (6 x 251 = 1506) but not Sessions II (1428 vs 1482) or III (1446 vs 1440), which supports the form's flag. Keeping rater counts in n_units with unit participant and leaving people counts null fits a design with no assignment of people to AI.

All ten 'reported' strings match the PDF digit for digit, checked on the page images and the text layer: Table 1 averages, standard errors, and Subj. (p. 7); Table 2 AI and AI_open coefficients, brackets, and Observations 494, 473, 474 in cols. (1), (4), (7) (p. 8); Table 3 originality averages and standard errors (p. 9); gaps 0.805, 1.046, 1.396 and 1.158, 0.517, 0.478 (p. 7); difference-in-difference 1.963, 1.563, 1.874 (p. 6).

One-line finding: closed 6.136 vs 5.331, 6.982 vs 5.936, 7.417 vs 6.021; open 5.108 vs 6.266, 5.933 vs 6.451, 6.451 vs 6.927; AI_open -1.943, -1.563, -1.875, all marked *** (significant at 1%) (p. 7, Table 1; p. 8, Table 2).

Measure details: 1-10 creativity score (p. 5); Sessions II and III add how unusual, well-elaborated, and nonsensical each answer was (p. 6); Table 2 regresses the average score on AI, Open, AI_open and temperature, with errors clustered at the subject-response level, subject-FE columns (2), (5), (8), and rwolf Romano-Wolf MHT columns (3), (6), (9) (pp. 7-8).

AI tool and task: temperature 0 to 2 set the same across tasks and versions, length raised from 256 to 400, and the Session III prompt adds 'Please be as creative as possible.' (p. 5 and fn. 7; p. 6). Both task prompts are quoted verbatim (pp. 5-6). The human producers had tournament incentives (pp. 5-6).
Participant quotes are verbatim: the 738-subject sentence and the Session II and Session III sentences (p. 4, Section 2.1).

Notes: fn. 8 reports five answers excluded for illegible scans (p. 6), and whether the open pool then holds 40 or 35 answers is ambiguous, so the flag is fair. The AsPredicted numbers (p. 1), Tables C4-C7 for Section 4 (p. 15), and subject-response clustering (p. 8) check out. company_involvement false (University of Milano funding, p. 1) and empty data_and_code (no data or code URL in the text) are right.

Preregistrations read online (AsPredicted #136955, #194851, #225528): the key dependent variables are creativity levels, plus originality, elaboration, and nonsense in the two follow-ups; each plans about 120 raters per treatment and states 'All observations will be included in the analysis.'
summary: The form rightly treats c039 as AI-versus-human context with no randomized study of people using AI: blind Prolific raters scored 2019 lab students' answers against GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, and GPT-4.5 answers, and every number in the reported strings, notes, and one-line finding matches Tables 1 to 3 and the text of the January 21, 2026 manuscript. The corrections concern structured fields: sample_overlap should name Charness and Grieco (2019), the creativity score is the paper's stated and preregistered main outcome, the preregistration, statistics_available, and criterion 1 fields are blank, the human producers are lab students rather than an online panel, the Session II closed-task originality direction is not supported, and one supplement locator is incomplete.
